meta.title: Clankers Made Me Build a Second Brain
meta.author: Tymscar

comments.author: swannodette
comments.text: I use a single linear date sorted Emacs org-mode notes.org file backed up to SourceHut. All notes are created with org-capture. Anything I want to remember how I did before, I can use consult-line to find answers quickly. Add a couple tags and I don't bother with organizing anything at all, org-sparse-tree for exploring. I have film recommendations, links to read, music to listen to mixed in with how to use Gnus, shell tricks, and less common Emacs commands, etc. I picked this habit about a year ago in response to the rapidly degrading quality of search and to counter the habit of reaching for a LLM for things I should really learn to do by heart.

comments.author: bityard
comments.text:
I've been using wiki software for my own "second brain" for at least a decade now, probably more. I have written hundreds (maybe thousands) of pages at this point. I cannot recommend it highly enough: If you are a knowledge worker, you cannot possibly hold everything in memory. Those who claim they can, are fooling themselves. (The greatest engineers/scientists/researchers throughout the centuries were also incredibly habitual writers and note-takers, and I don't think this is a coincidence.)

Plus, the act of writing something down makes it more likely than not you will remember it (or at least, remember it better). At a certain point, having it available for later reference is almost more of a side-benefit.

I eventually just wrote my own knowledge base for the improved UX/ergonomics. (I'm a big fan of search over metadata curation.) The current version is entirely coded by hand because most of it was written before AI could write code competently enough for my taste, although I am looking at experimenting with some potential improvements using locally-hosted models in the very near future.

comments.author: judson
comments.text: Better than Obsidian notes is to put it into your Anki deck (for flashcard review / spaced repetition) and have it memorized and always on your mental cache

comments.author: z3bra
comments.text:
I find taking note solo hard. I always end up turning "quick notes" into a blog post, which takes me out of the current flow.

My idea off taking notes is a keybind that pops an editor, I scribble a quick line, eg. « put 2>&1 before >/dev/null », replay the keybind, and have it archived somehow, so that later on, I can use a fuzzy finder to look up « /dev/null » and have the note pop up.

This part is actually easy to implement, but this get harder when you want to browse the notes later on. I'd be eager to know how people organize their note, and find their way back...

Right now I just resort to writing shell scripts and comment them out, then grep -r ~/bin to get answers. Only works for shell tricks though.

comments.author: tonyarkles
comments.text: My current note-taking and task capture flow is a mix of Obsidian+Todoist+Raycast. I have cmd-shift-o as a global Raycast shortcut for “create inbox task” and cmd+shift+p as “quick add to daily note” which appends a timestamped entry to “Daily Notes/2026-09-24.md” in my Obsidian vault. It’s imperfect. My Todoist inbox is a disaster right now and I’ve started adding extra keywords/tags to my daily note quick captures to make them more searchable, but overall it’s working a lot better than writing stuff on paper and completely forgetting it.

comments.author: notgull
comments.text: This article mentions it, but what's the best way to organize notes in Obsidian? It implies a structure that can be used to help retain ideas.

comments.author: tonyarkles
comments.text:
The best way to organize notes in Obsidian is whatever works best for you. The primary developer of obsidian doesn’t really use folders much at all. I do somewhat loosely. Other people get much more structured like… hmm I think it was called Johnny Decimal?

Just play around and figure out what works for you. Search works pretty good. Tags work well. The data table stuff works great for some people.

comments.author: npiazza
comments.text:
100% this. Start small and experiment. Don’t get bogged down with third party plugins to start.

Once you get comfortable, play with your Daily Note template.

Obsidian is one of the programs like Vim that have stepwise learning curves. Use it until you personally run into a problem that annoys you, then just try to solve just that problem.

Personally, I’ve slimmed down to using links exclusively over tags. Whenever I write a proper noun, I’ll make a link to it at least once in the note. I avoid folders except for special cases. Once I used my notebook for more than a year, I found it useful to have my daily notes use [automatic subfolders)(https://obsidian.md/help/plugins/daily-notes#:~:text=Automatic%20subfolders) (expand that dropdown)

If you pin the [local graph view](https://obsidian.md/help/plugins/graph#Local+Graph] you can see a relationship show up organically by seeing only close neighbors to your current note.

comments.author: hono4kami
comments.text:
Make it as flat as possible, IMO. Personally my vault is structured flat like this

notes/
├─ 2026-01-01-00-00-bash-string-substition.md
├─ 2026-01-02-00-00-zig-async-io.md
├─ 2026-01-02-00-00-go-concurrency.md
media/
├─ 20260101000000.jpeg
Zig.md
Bash.md
Data-oriented Design.md
Entity component system.md
Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs.md


There are no more folders beyond this, there are no folders nested inside. The root folder is for my Wiki pages that doubles as topic that can be referenced inside the notes/ folder. Only files inside notes/ can call Wiki pages, the Wiki pages can not reference  notes/. The way it works is, say on 2026-01-01-00-00-bash-string-substition.md, the content of the note is:

How to do string substition in [[Bash]].

a="lorem dolor amet";
echo "${a/dolor/ipsum}"; # lorem ipsum amet


That way when I open Bash.md and see the backlinks, I can see the list of notes that are related to Bash.

In other words, the wiki pages also works kind of like glossary. Or if you've been to a image board websites, it's kinda like tagging system inside many image boards.

comments.author: tonyarkles
comments.text:
I have a little more structure than that myself but not a ton. The knowledge-base part of it is very similar to what you’re doing in a somewhat nebulous “Notes on Things” folder. I’ve also got a “Daily Notes” folder where a 2026-09-24.md gets created the first time I capture a “Quick Note” in Raycast (or hit the Daily Note button in Obsidian). I’ve also got per-project folders for the different work and personal stuff I’m working on with things like design notes, todo lists, etc. so that a project can sit on a shelf for a while and I can pick it back up when I have time.

I think the best way I can say it, which agrees with you in large part: “Keep it as flat as possible, but no flatter”

comments.author: vetch
comments.text: I found the book "Taking smart notes" to be a good read - I don't follow the exact implementation they have, and it is obsidian agnostic. Having a logging  -> notes distillation process has been good for me. Logging is both online and offline depending on the day and notes should be fairly well back linked to make it easier to find related ideas.
